title: The Land Not Taken
sum: After Joshua's death the tribes ask the LORD who should go first, and Judah leads. Judah and Simeon defeat Adoni-bezek, who admits that God has paid him back (1:1–7). Judah takes Jerusalem, Hebron and Debir; Caleb's daughter Achsah asks for springs of water; the Kenites settle in the Negev; Zephath becomes Hormah (1:8–20). Then the tone changes. Benjamin does not drive out the Jebusites, and the house of Joseph takes Bethel only by sparing a traitor (1:21–26). Tribe after tribe, from Manasseh to Dan, fails to drive out the Canaanites, and the list ends with the Danites pushed into the hills (1:27–36).

The chapter is a report card. It begins with "the LORD was with Judah" and ends with Canaanites living on in Israel, set to forced labor instead of being driven out. Much of it repeats lists from Joshua 15–17, but here the failures are gathered in one place, and the next chapter will explain them.
readings: Read as a conquest record

Read this way, the chapter fills in what happened after Joshua: some real gains in the south, and a long frontier of Canaanite cities that held out. Archaeology agrees that cities in the valleys, such as Megiddo, Beth-shean and Gezer, stayed Canaanite or under Egyptian control well into the twelfth century BC.
Read as a decline

Read as literature, the chapter slides from Judah's success to Dan's defeat, and from the south to the north. Judah "took possession"; Manasseh "did not"; Dan was pushed back. The order is not just geographic: it is the first turn of a spiral that ends with Dan's idols (chapter 18) and Benjamin's near-destruction (chapters 20–21).

views.H: Traditional readers see the chapter as an honest record of partial success. Judah's victories show what faith could do; the other tribes' failures were real, and they explain why Israel lived among Canaanites for centuries, until David took Jerusalem.
views.C: Many scholars think chapter 1 is an older, more realistic account of the settlement than Joshua 1–12, built from tribal traditions and the notes in Joshua 15–17. Its list of unconquered cities matches the archaeological picture of a slow and partial settlement in the hills. Others see it as a late introduction, written to show the tribes, except Judah, failing.
views.L: Literary readers watch Judah's favored place: Judah goes first here and in 20:18. Adoni-bezek's mutilation and confession set up the book's theme of measure-for-measure justice. Achsah is the first of the book's women, and she is the most secure: married by her father's promise, she asks and receives. Later women will fare worse.
views.J: The rabbis noted that Judah took Jerusalem (1:8) and yet the Jebusites remained (1:21); some said the city's outer parts were taken while the stronghold held out until David. Othniel was honored as the first judge and a great teacher of Torah (Bavli Temurah 16a).
views.X: Christian readers have drawn moral lessons from the failure to drive out the Canaanites: compromise with sin leaves enemies within. Origen's homilies read the conquest of the land as the soul's struggle against vice.

deep.b: Several verses in this chapter repeat Joshua almost word for word. Achsah's story (1:11–15) matches Joshua 15:15–19; the note on Jerusalem (1:21) matches Joshua 15:63, except that there it was Judah who "could not drive out" the Jebusites, and here it is Benjamin. Gezer (1:29) matches Joshua 16:10, and Manasseh's list (1:27–28) matches Joshua 17:11–13. Joshua says Caleb "drove out" the three sons of Anak himself (Joshua 15:14), while Judges 1:10 credits Judah. These differences show that the editors of both books drew on shared lists, shaping them to their own purposes. In Joshua the gaps are exceptions to a great conquest; in Judges they are the main story.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Adoni-bezek as the book in miniature
deep.b: My own reading: the first enemy in Judges speaks the book's theology more clearly than any Israelite. He loses his thumbs and toes, as he cut off the thumbs and toes of seventy kings, and he says that God has repaid him. Seventy returns in chapter 9, where Abimelech kills seventy brothers and God repays him (9:56). A table with scraps beneath it returns, in a darker form, in Samson's grinding and the Levite's meal before the outrage at Gibeah. I suggest the editor placed Adoni-bezek first so that a Canaanite king states the rule that will judge Israel itself: what you do comes back. Scholars note the measure-for-measure pattern; the frame of seventy to seventy is my own suggestion.

echoes: Joshua 15:13–19; Joshua 15:63; Joshua 16:10; Joshua 17:11–13; Numbers 21:1–3; Genesis 49:8–12; Deuteronomy 7:1–5; 2 Samuel 5:6–9; 20:18

settings.what: The LORD names Judah to go first
settings.by: The Israelites, and the LORD in answer
settings.to: The LORD, asked by the tribes, probably at a sanctuary by lot
settings.when: after Joshua's death, with no leader in his place
settings.why: With no successor to Joshua, the tribes ask God who will lead the fight. The answer is Judah. The same question and answer come back in 20:18, but then the fight is against Benjamin. For readers under the kings of Judah, the book opens with Judah leading.

title: Weeping at Bochim
sum: The angel of the LORD comes up from Gilgal to Bochim and charges Israel with breaking covenant: they made deals with the land's people and did not pull down their altars, so God will not drive the nations out (2:1–5). The story then steps back to Joshua's death and burial. The generation that had seen the LORD's work serves him, but a new generation grows up "that knew nothing of the LORD, or of the work he had done for Israel" (2:6–10).

Then comes the book's program. Israel serves the Baals; God hands them to raiders; they groan; God raises up judges who rescue them; the judge dies and they sink lower than before (2:11–19). So God will leave the nations in place as a test (2:20–23). Every story that follows is a turn of this wheel.
readings: Read as a sermon

The chapter interprets history before telling it. Like a preacher's outline, it gives the pattern first: sin, punishment, cry, rescue, rest, and worse sin. The reader is meant to see each judge's story as proof.
Read as a generational story

The key word is "know." The first generation knew the LORD's work; the next did not. Faith did not pass to the children. Many readers find this the chapter's lasting challenge to parents and communities.

views.H: Traditional readers see the cycle as God's real dealings with Israel over two centuries, and Bochim as a real assembly where Israel repented with tears, though briefly.
views.C: For Martin Noth and most critical scholars, 2:6–3:6 is the clearest work of the Deuteronomistic editor: its vocabulary ("did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD," "sold them," "the LORD's anger blazed") matches Deuteronomy and Kings. Joshua 24:28–31 is repeated in 2:6–9 to join the books. The cycle is a frame laid over older hero stories.
views.L: Literary readers notice that the cycle is not static. It is a spiral: "they would go back and behave worse than their ancestors" (2:19). Later stories break the pattern: no crying out in chapter 9, no rescue in Samson's story, and in chapters 17–21 no judge at all.
views.J: The rabbis identified the angel of 2:1 with Phinehas the priest, since a messenger who speaks God's word can be a prophet (Leviticus Rabbah 1:1). Bochim, "the weepers," was linked with other national days of mourning.
views.X: Christian readers apply the cycle to the life of the church and of each believer: forgetting, falling, crying out, and grace. The need for one rescuer who does not die, and so does not leave the people to slide back, is read as pointing to Christ (Hebrews 7:23–25).

deep.b: Judges 2:6–9 repeats Joshua 24:28–31 with small changes. Joshua says the elders were "men who knew all that the LORD had done for Israel" (Joshua 24:31); Judges says they "had seen the whole great work" (2:7). The repetition is a common ancient way to begin a new section of a history by restating where the last one ended. It also sets up 2:10: the elders had seen; the next generation "knew nothing of the LORD." Joshua's burial place is spelled Timnath-serah in Joshua and Timnath-heres in Judges; the letters are reversed, and "heres" means "sun."

deep.title: Claude's theory: Bochim and the Weeping of chapter 20
deep.b: My own reading: the book opens and closes with Israel weeping before God near Bethel. At Bochim they weep after being told the nations will stay (2:4–5); at Bethel they weep after civil war has nearly wiped out Benjamin (20:23, 26; 21:2). If the Greek is right that Bochim was near Bethel, the book's frame is a place of tears, and the weeping at the end answers the weeping at the start: the nations within have become Israel itself. The link of Bochim to Bethel is old; the reading of the two scenes as a deliberate frame is my own.

echoes: Joshua 23:12–13; Joshua 24:28–31; Exodus 23:32–33; Exodus 34:12–13; Numbers 33:55; Deuteronomy 7:2–5; Deuteronomy 31:16–18; Psalm 78:56–58; Psalm 106:34–45; Nehemiah 9:26–28

settings.to: The Israelites gathered at Bochim, perhaps near Bethel (the Greek adds Bethel)
settings.when: after the tribes fail to drive out the Canaanites
settings.why: The angel says that God kept his covenant, but Israel made deals with the people of the land and did not tear down their altars. So God will not drive them out, and their gods will become a trap. The people weep, and the place is named Bochim, Weepers. The speech explains to later readers why Canaanites lived on in Israel.

settings.what: The LORD's verdict: the nations will stay
settings.to: No one: the narrator reports God's decision about Israel, in the third person (compare 2:1–5, where the angel speaks to Israel)
settings.when: after the first generations turn to the Baals
settings.why: Because Israel broke the covenant, God will not drive out the nations left after Joshua. They will stay to test Israel. The verdict frames every story that follows.

title: Othniel, Ehud and Shamgar
sum: The nations left to test Israel are named, and Israel intermarries with them and serves their gods (3:1–6). Then come the first three judges. Othniel, Caleb's younger brother (or nephew; see 1:13), is the model: Israel cries out, the Spirit comes on him, he defeats Cushan-rishathaim, and the land rests forty years (3:7–11). Ehud the left-handed Benjaminite brings tribute to the fat king Eglon of Moab, kills him in his private room with a hidden sword, escapes while the servants wait outside, and leads Israel to seize the Jordan fords (3:12–30). Shamgar strikes six hundred Philistines with an ox goad (3:31).

Othniel's short account uses every part of the pattern of chapter 2 and adds nothing, as if to show the system working. Ehud's story is the opposite: full of detail, humor and gore, with no mention of the Spirit.
readings: Read as a model and a comedy

Othniel is the template; Ehud is the first variation. Ehud's story is told as a comic tale of an enemy king outwitted, with puns on "tribute" and "fat," a locked toilet room and embarrassed servants. Israel's audience would have laughed.
Read as a moral problem

Ehud kills by deceit, using God's name as bait: "I have a word from God for you." The narrator says the LORD raised him up (3:15), and Calvin counted such judges as avengers God raised against tyrants. But the text never says God told him to use the sword this way, and Lillian Klein and Susan Niditch read the tale as ironic trickster satire rather than a model.

views.H: Traditional readers place Othniel early in the period, soon after Joshua, since he is Caleb's younger brother (or nephew; see 1:13). Eglon's control of Jericho ("the City of Palms") and Ehud's escape to the hill country fit the geography of Benjamin and Moab.
views.C: Critical scholars find Cushan-rishathaim, "Cushan of double wickedness," hard to place; some think Aram is a slip for Edom. They see Othniel's story as an editorial model built from stock phrases. Ehud's story is old Benjaminite tradition, kept close to its oral form.
views.L: Literary readers love Ehud's story for its craft: the left hand, the hidden sword, the fat that closes over the blade, the servants who wait "until they felt ashamed." The first foreign king in the book dies in a toilet; the last major judge will die in a Philistine temple.
views.J: The rabbis praised Eglon for one act: he rose from his throne when Ehud said he had a word from God (3:20). As a reward, they said, Ruth the Moabite, Eglon's descendant in their tradition, became an ancestor of David (Ruth Rabbah 2:9).
views.X: Hebrews does not name Othniel or Ehud, but Christian writers have taken Ehud's two-edged sword as a picture of God's word, "sharper than any two-mouthed sword" (Hebrews 4:12). Othniel, on whom the Spirit came, was read as a figure of Christ anointed by the Spirit.

deep.b: Ehud is "a man hampered in his right hand," literally "bound" in it. In 20:16 Benjamin has seven hundred elite troops who were "bound in the right hand" and could sling a stone at a hair. Some think these men were trained from youth to use the left hand, by binding the right, because left-handed fighters had an advantage: guards searched the left side, where a right-handed man carried his weapon. The irony is that Benjamin means "son of the right hand." Ehud's handicap becomes his weapon.

deep.title: Claude's theory: three judges as three ways of rescue
deep.b: My own reading: chapter 3 offers three kinds of deliverer in quick succession. Othniel rescues by the Spirit, in a story with no detail at all. Ehud rescues by cunning, in a story with nothing but detail. Shamgar rescues by brute force with a farm tool, in one verse. The book seems to be showing the range of God's instruments before testing each one: the Spirit will come on Gideon, Jephthah and Samson; cunning returns with Jael and Gideon's night attack; and the farmer's tools return in Gideon's threshing and Samson's jawbone. Scholars often contrast Othniel and Ehud; the threefold pattern is my own suggestion.

echoes: Joshua 15:17; Deuteronomy 7:3–4; Exodus 34:15–16; 1 Samuel 12:9–11; 20:16; Hebrews 4:12; Nehemiah 9:27

settings.by: Ehud son of Gera, a left-handed Benjaminite
settings.to: Eglon king of Moab, alone in his upper room
settings.when: after Ehud brings Israel's tribute
settings.why: "I have a word from God for you" is a trick, and also true: the word is a sword. Readers in Israel would hear it as a joke at the expense of an oppressor.

title: Deborah, Barak and Jael
sum: After Ehud's death Israel sins again, and Jabin king of Canaan, ruling from Hazor, oppresses them for twenty years with nine hundred iron chariots. His commander is Sisera (4:1–3). Deborah, a prophet who judges Israel under a palm tree, summons Barak and gives him God's order to gather ten thousand men at Mount Tabor. Barak will go only if she goes. She agrees, but warns that the glory will go to a woman (4:4–10).

The LORD throws Sisera's army into panic at the Kishon, and Sisera flees on foot to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite. She welcomes him, gives him milk, covers him, and drives a tent peg through his head while he sleeps. Barak arrives to find him dead (4:11–22). God brings Jabin low, and Israel's hand presses on him until he is destroyed (4:23–24).
readings: Read as a story of women

The chapter turns on two women. Deborah leads Israel with God's word; Jael finishes the battle with a peg. Barak, the man who should be the hero, is told the glory will not be his. Many readers, from the rabbis to modern feminist critics, have made this the chapter's main point.
Read as holy war

The real warrior is the LORD: he draws Sisera out, he marches ahead, he throws the army into panic. Barak and his men pursue a beaten enemy. The poem of chapter 5 adds that the stars and the river fought too.

views.H: Traditional readers locate the battle in the Jezreel Valley, near Mount Tabor and the Kishon. Some note that Joshua had already burned Hazor and killed a Jabin (Joshua 11:10–13), and suggest a later king of the same dynasty, or that Hazor was rebuilt.
views.C: Critical scholars compare the prose account with the older poem of chapter 5 and find differences: the poem names more tribes and does not mention Jabin. Many think Jabin was added from Joshua 11 and that the prose was written from the poem. Excavations at Hazor show its great Canaanite city destroyed in the thirteenth century BC.
views.L: Literary readers note how often the story reverses roles: a woman judges, a man hesitates, a woman offers hospitality and kills. Sisera tells Jael to say "No" if anyone asks whether there is a man here (4:20); there soon is not.
views.J: The rabbis honored Deborah as one of seven women prophets (Bavli Megillah 14a), though some were uneasy with her pride and her calling Barak rather than going to him. The Talmud praised Jael, saying a sin done for the sake of heaven, like hers, is greater than a good deed done for other reasons (Bavli Nazir 23b).
views.X: Hebrews 11:32 names Barak among the heroes of faith, not Deborah or Jael. Christian writers have honored Deborah as a woman leader, and Jael's "blessed above women" has long been compared with Mary's greeting in Luke 1:42.

deep.b: Nine hundred iron chariots sound unbeatable, and they explain why the tribes could not take the valleys (1:19). Chariots were probably made of wood with iron fittings, and they needed firm, dry ground. The poem says the Kishon "swept them away" (5:21), and many readers have pictured a sudden storm turning the valley floor to mud, so that the chariots stuck and their crews fled on foot, as Sisera did (4:15). The prose says only that the LORD threw them into panic.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the milk and the mother
deep.b: My own reading: Jael's act is framed in motherly terms. She covers Sisera, gives him milk instead of water, and watches over him like a child put to bed. The poem then turns to Sisera's real mother, waiting at the window (5:28), while Deborah calls herself "a mother in Israel" (5:7). I suggest the narrator sets three mothers side by side: Deborah who protects Israel, Jael who plays mother to destroy, and Sisera's mother who will wait in vain. Scholars have noted the maternal images in the poem; reading them as a deliberate threefold set is my own.

echoes: Joshua 11:1–13; Exodus 14:24–25; Exodus 15:20–21; 1 Samuel 12:9–11; Psalm 83:9–10; Luke 1:42; Hebrews 11:32

settings.what: Deborah summons Barak and sends him to battle
settings.by: Deborah, a prophet who judged Israel
settings.to: Barak son of Abinoam, from Kedesh in Naphtali
settings.when: after twenty years of oppression by Jabin and his chariots
settings.why: Deborah gives Barak God's order to gather ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun at Mount Tabor. Barak will go only if she goes. She agrees, but warns that the glory will go to a woman. At Mount Tabor she tells him that today the LORD has marched out ahead of him (4:14). The speech turns the story: the battle is the LORD's, and the hero will not be the general.

settings.what: Jael's words to Sisera and Barak
settings.by: Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, and Sisera
settings.to: Sisera, then Barak
settings.when: as Sisera flees on foot after the battle
settings.why: Jael welcomes Sisera with "Do not be afraid," and he asks her to lie for him. She kills him and shows Barak the man he is looking for. Her words of welcome are a trap, and Deborah's warning comes true.

traditions.q: Does Deborah show that women may lead and preach in the church?
views: Deborah was a true prophet and judge, and women may serve the Church in many ways. But only baptized men may be ordained priests, because Christ chose men as his apostles, and John Paul II declared that the Church has no authority to ordain women (Catechism 1577; Ordinatio Sacerdotalis).

The Orthodox honor women prophets and saints, some of them called equal to the apostles, but ordain only men as priests and bishops. Whether to restore the ancient order of women deacons is still discussed.

Southern Baptists hold that the office of pastor is limited to men (Baptist Faith and Message, article 6), and many read Deborah as a special case in a time when men like Barak failed to lead. Other Baptist bodies, such as the American Baptist Churches, ordain women.

Pentecostals have licensed women preachers from the start, since the Spirit falls on sons and daughters alike (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17). The Assemblies of God points to Deborah as proof that God calls women to lead his people (The Role of Women in Ministry).
Methodists ordain women. John Wesley allowed some women with an extraordinary call to preach, and the main Methodist church in the United States has given women full clergy rights since 1956.

Lutherans are divided. The Evangelical Lutheran Church in America and many Lutheran churches around the world ordain women, while the Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod holds that the pastoral office belongs to men only (1 Timothy 2:12).
Anglicans are divided. The Church of England has ordained women as priests since 1994 and as bishops since 2015, while several Anglican provinces do not ordain women as priests.

title: The Song of Deborah
sum: Deborah and Barak sing the victory. The LORD marches from Seir and the earth shakes (5:2–5). In Shamgar's and Jael's days the roads were empty and village life died, until Deborah rose up, a mother in Israel (5:6–11). The tribes are called: Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun, Issachar and Naphtali come; Reuben, Gilead, Dan and Asher stay home, and Meroz is cursed for not helping (5:12–18, 23). Kings fight at Taanach, the stars fight from heaven, and the Kishon sweeps the enemy away (5:19–22).

Jael is blessed above women: she gives milk, then strikes with the peg, and Sisera falls between her feet (5:24–27). At the window Sisera's mother waits, and her ladies imagine the plunder he must be dividing (5:28–30). The song ends with a prayer: may God's enemies perish, and those who love him shine like the rising sun (5:31).
readings: Read as ancient poetry

Most scholars think the Song of Deborah is among the oldest poems in the Bible, perhaps from the twelfth century BC. Its archaic grammar, its rough repetitions and its tribal roll call fit an early Israel of separate tribes without a king.
Read as a theology of victory

The poem calls the battle "the LORD's just deeds" (5:11) and gives credit to God, the stars and the river. The human volunteers are praised and the stay-at-homes shamed, but the LORD is the one who marches.

views.H: Traditional readers take the song as Deborah's own composition, sung on the day of victory (5:1), a second account of chapter 4 in poetic form.
views.C: Critical scholars mostly date the song early, before the prose of chapter 4, and see it as a key source for the history of Israel's tribes. Its list of ten tribes, without Judah, Simeon or Levi, suggests a time before the twelve-tribe system was fixed. Lawrence Stager has linked the tribes who stayed home to their trade and coast-based economies.
views.L: Literary readers praise the song's repetition and slow motion: "he bent down, he fell, he lay" (5:27). The final scene of Sisera's mother is one of the most daring in the Bible: the poem asks us to see the enemy's mother waiting, and lets the irony do the rest.
views.J: The song is the haftarah for the Sabbath of Song (Beshallach), read with the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15). The rabbis counted it among the ten great songs of history. The Targum expands it greatly with the history of Israel.
views.X: Christian readers compared the song with Miriam's and Mary's songs (Exodus 15; Luke 1:46–55) and read its ending, those who love God shining like the sun, alongside Matthew 13:43.

deep.h: Who came and who stayed home
deep.b: The roll call (5:14–18) is a rare glimpse of the tribes acting, or not, as a group. Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir (part of Manasseh), Zebulun, Issachar and Naphtali came. Reuben debated and stayed among the sheep; Gilead stayed east of the Jordan; Dan stayed by the ships; Asher sat by the sea. Judah and Simeon are not mentioned at all. Some scholars think the south was not yet part of the league; others think the poem lists only the tribes near the battle. Dan is placed by the sea, which suits its first home near Joppa before the move north in chapter 18.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the song's mirror at the window
deep.b: My own reading: the song begins and ends with women who interpret events. Deborah "rose up, a mother in Israel" and sings the true meaning of the battle; Sisera's mother looks out the window and her wise ladies give the false meaning: plunder, women, dyed cloth. The poem sets two "mothers" and two interpretations against each other. I suggest that the song's point is not only who won but who reads the event rightly: "the LORD's just deeds" (5:11) against "a womb or two for every man" (5:30). Scholars have often contrasted Deborah and Sisera's mother; seeing the contrast as two rival readings of history is my own suggestion.

echoes: Exodus 15:1–21; Deuteronomy 33:2; Psalm 68:7–8; Psalm 68:17; Habakkuk 3:3–6; Joshua 10:12–14; 2 Samuel 22:8–16; Luke 1:42; Luke 1:46–55

settings.to: The LORD, the kings and rulers called to listen (5:3), and the tribes of Israel, both those who came and those who stayed home
settings.when: on the day of the victory over Sisera at the Kishon
settings.why: The Song praises the LORD who marched from Seir and fought from the sky. It praises the tribes who offered themselves freely. It shames Reuben, Gilead, Dan and Asher for staying home and curses Meroz. Jael is blessed above women. At the end it mocks Sisera's mother waiting at the window. A victory song was meant to be sung again, at the watering places (5:11). It would bind the tribes together and honor those who risked their lives. Hearing who is praised and who is shamed tells readers what loyalty looked like when there was no king.
views: Many scholars date the Song to the 12th or 11th century BC, close to the events. They point to its old Hebrew and its picture of a loose league of tribes without Judah.
Others think it was written or reshaped much later, using old forms. Serge Frolov dates it to the late exile or just after, in the 6th century BC.
Feminist and other readers note that the poem is framed by women: Deborah the "mother in Israel," Jael, and Sisera's mother.

title: Gideon Called
sum: Israel sins, and for seven years Midian and the eastern peoples swarm in like locusts at harvest, stripping the land; Israel hides in caves (6:1–6). When they cry out, a prophet reminds them of the Exodus and their disobedience (6:7–10). The angel of the LORD sits under the oak at Ophrah and greets Gideon, who is threshing wheat in a winepress, as a mighty fighter. Gideon objects and asks for a sign; fire from the rock consumes his offering, and he builds an altar called "The LORD Is Peace" (6:11–24).

That night Gideon pulls down his father's Baal altar and Asherah pole. The town wants him dead, but his father Joash says Baal can defend himself, and Gideon is named Jerubbaal (6:25–32). As Midian gathers in the Jezreel Valley, the Spirit clothes Gideon, and he calls the tribes. Then he tests God twice with a fleece (6:33–40).
readings: Read as a call story

Gideon's call follows the pattern of Moses' call (Exodus 3–4): a divine meeting, an objection of weakness, a promise of presence ("I will be with you"), and a sign. Like Moses, Gideon becomes a reluctant rescuer.
Read as a story of doubt
Gideon questions, delays and asks for proof again and again. Some readers see faith growing slowly through God's patience; others see a doubter whose need for signs foreshadows his later failures.

views.H: Traditional readers take Midian's raids as historical: camel-riding nomads from the eastern desert swept through the farmland at harvest. Gideon's family in Manasseh, with its Baal altar, reflects real religious mixing in Israel's villages.
views.C: Critical scholars note signs of more than one source: Gideon and Jerubbaal may once have been different heroes, and the prophet's speech (6:7–10) is missing from a Qumran fragment. The name "Jerubbaal" probably meant "Baal contends" or "may Baal be great" before being reinterpreted. Domesticated camels are rare in the archaeological record of the land before about the tenth century BC, which some take as a sign of a later telling.
views.L: Literary readers enjoy the irony of "mighty fighter" addressed to a man hiding in a winepress. Gideon starts the chapter afraid of Midian, then afraid of his own town (6:27), and ends it testing God. His courage grows, but his questions never fully stop.
views.J: The rabbis praised Gideon for defending Israel before God ("where are all his wonders?"), and said that God chose him for speaking up for his people (Rashi on 6:14). The Talmud lists Gideon with Samson and Jephthah as "the lightest" of leaders, yet says that Gideon in his generation was like Moses in his, and Jephthah like Samuel (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 25b).
views.X: Christian readers saw the dew on the fleece, then on the ground, as Israel first blessed, then the nations; others read the fleece wet while the ground was dry as the Virgin Mary receiving Christ. The angel's fire from the rock was read as a picture of Christ's acceptance of sacrifice.

deep.h: The fleece and asking for signs
deep.b: Gideon's fleece has become a common phrase for asking God for a sign. The text itself is careful: God has already promised (6:14, 16), and Gideon twice asks for confirmation, apologizing the second time ("Do not let your anger blaze against me"). Deuteronomy warns not to put the LORD to the test (Deuteronomy 6:16), and Jesus quotes that verse (Matthew 4:7). Yet God answers Gideon's tests without rebuke, and gives him another sign unasked in the dream of chapter 7. Many readers conclude that God bears with weak faith, without making Gideon's method a rule.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two altars and two names
deep.b: My own reading: chapter 6 has two altars and two names, and they mirror each other. Gideon's first altar, "The LORD Is Peace," comes from a private meeting; his second, on the stronghold, replaces Baal's in public. His first name, Gideon, means "hacker" or "cutter"; he earns it by cutting down the Asherah. His second, Jerubbaal, "Let Baal contend," is given by his father as a dare to Baal. I suggest the chapter is built so that each name matches an act. Scholars widely note the meaning of Gideon's name; the pairing of the two names with the two altars is my own suggestion.

echoes: Exodus 3:1–4:17; Exodus 33:20; Genesis 18:1–8; Deuteronomy 6:16; Deuteronomy 7:5; Judges 13:15–23; 1 Kings 18:20–40; Isaiah 9:4; Isaiah 10:26

settings.to: The Israelites, crying out under Midian
settings.when: after seven years of Midianite raids
settings.why: Before God sends a rescuer, he sends a prophet. He recalls the exodus and the command not to fear the gods of the Amorites. He ends, "you have not listened to my voice." The speech makes Israel's cry a call to repent, not only for relief.

settings.by: The angel of the LORD, and Gideon
settings.to: Gideon son of Joash, threshing wheat in a winepress at Ophrah
settings.when: in the time of Midian
settings.why: The angel greets Gideon as a mighty fighter. Gideon objects: where are the wonders our ancestors told us of? God promises to be with him. Gideon asks for a sign, and fire from the rock consumes his offering. He builds an altar called "The LORD Is Peace." The call shows God choosing the least in the smallest clan. For readers, Gideon's question is their own whenever God seems absent.

settings.to: Gideon
settings.when: that same night
settings.why: God orders Gideon to tear down his father's altar to Baal and the Asherah pole, and build an altar to the LORD. Before he can rescue Israel from Midian, he must break with Baal at home.

settings.to: The men of Ophrah who want Gideon dead
settings.when: the morning after the altar is torn down
settings.why: Joash says that if Baal is a god, he can fight for himself. The words give Gideon the name Jerubbaal and mock Baal before the town.

settings.to: God
settings.when: as Midian gathers in the Jezreel Valley
settings.why: Gideon asks for two signs with a fleece, wet and then dry. God gives them. The prayer shows Gideon's fear, and God's patience with him.

title: Three Hundred Against Midian
sum: Gideon's army camps at the spring of Harod facing Midian. God says it is too big: Israel would boast. The fearful go home, leaving ten thousand; then a drinking test at the water leaves three hundred (7:1–8). God sends Gideon to spy on the camp, where he overhears a Midianite telling his dream of a barley loaf flattening a tent, and his friend explaining it as "the sword of Gideon." Gideon worships (7:9–15).

He divides his men into three companies with horns, jars and torches. At the middle watch they blow, smash the jars, raise the torches and shout. The enemy turn their swords on each other and flee (7:16–22). Gideon calls out the tribes, and Ephraim seizes the Jordan fords and kills the Midianite commanders Oreb and Zeeb (7:23–25).
readings: Read as faith
God shrinks the army so the victory can only be his. The story's lesson, repeated by Jonathan, Zechariah and Paul, is that God saves by few as well as by many.
Read as a war tale

Read as a soldier's story, it is a brilliant night raid: a small force, total surprise, noise and light to spread panic in a sleeping camp of nomads. Ancient writers on strategy record similar tricks.

views.H: Traditional readers see the battle as a real night attack in the Jezreel Valley, with God's help seen both in the dream and in the enemy's panic. The geography, from Harod to the Jordan crossings, fits well.
views.C: Critical scholars find two strands: one where the men carry horns, another where they carry jars and torches, which would need three hands (7:20). The story may combine a tradition of Gideon's clan, Abiezer, with a wider Israelite muster. The huge numbers are probably not literal.
views.L: Literary readers watch Gideon's fear: God offers him a cure for it ("if you are afraid," 7:10), and Gideon goes. The dream is told by the enemy, which makes Midian the one who announces its own defeat. The battle cry adds Gideon's name to God's.
views.J: The rabbis taught that the merit of the omer, the barley offering, won the battle, reading the barley loaf of the dream as the omer (Leviticus Rabbah 28:6). Isaiah later recalls "the day of Midian" as the model of God breaking an oppressor's yoke (Isaiah 9:4).
views.X: Christian preachers have read the torches hidden in clay jars as the light of the gospel carried in fragile human bodies (2 Corinthians 4:7), shining out when the jar is broken. Hebrews 11:32 names Gideon first among the judges it lists.

deep.b: The idea that God gives victory to the few runs through Israel's story. Jonathan tells his armor-bearer that the LORD "can save with many or with few" (1 Samuel 14:6). Asa prays that it is nothing for God to help the weak against the strong (2 Chronicles 14:11). Zechariah hears that the temple will be built not by might or force but by God's Spirit (Zechariah 4:6). Paul applies it to the church: God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong, so no one can boast (1 Corinthians 1:27–29). Gideon's three hundred became the classic illustration.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the dream as Gideon's last sign
deep.b: My own reading: chapters 6 and 7 give Gideon four signs: fire from the rock, the wet fleece, the dry fleece, and the dream. The first three he asks for; the fourth God offers without being asked, through the mouth of the enemy. I suggest the dream is placed last to close Gideon's season of testing God. After it, for the first time, he worships and gives orders without asking for proof (7:15). The barley loaf, poor farmer's bread, is Gideon himself, the threshing man from the winepress. Scholars widely note the signs; the idea that God's unasked sign ends the series is my own.

echoes: Deuteronomy 8:17–18; Deuteronomy 20:1–9; 1 Samuel 14:6; 2 Chronicles 20:22–23; Psalm 83:9–12; Isaiah 9:4; Isaiah 10:26; Zechariah 4:6; 1 Corinthians 1:27–29; 2 Corinthians 4:7

settings.to: Gideon, at the spring of Harod
settings.when: before the battle with Midian
settings.why: God says the army is too big; Israel would boast that its own hand saved it. The fearful go home, and a test at the water leaves three hundred. The words make sure the victory is clearly God's, as in Deuteronomy 20:8.

settings.by: The LORD; a Midianite soldier and his friend
settings.to: Gideon, sent down to the enemy camp, and listening
settings.when: the night of the attack
settings.why: God lets Gideon overhear a dream of a barley loaf flattening a tent, and the friend's reading: "the sword of Gideon." Gideon worships. God answers his fear by letting his enemies say it.

settings.to: His three hundred men, in three companies
settings.when: at the middle watch
settings.why: Gideon tells them to copy him and shout, "For the LORD and for Gideon!" The battle cry already shows Gideon's name beside God's, a hint of trouble to come.

title: Gideon's Revenge and Gideon's Ephod
sum: Ephraim complains that it was not called, and Gideon calms them with flattery (8:1–3). Crossing the Jordan after the kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, Gideon is refused bread at Succoth and Penuel and swears revenge. He captures the kings at Karkor, then flogs the elders of Succoth with thorns and tears down Penuel's tower, killing its men (8:4–17). He executes the two kings for killing his brothers at Tabor (8:18–21).

Israel asks Gideon to rule as a dynasty. He refuses: "The LORD will rule over you." But he asks for gold earrings from the plunder and makes an ephod, which all Israel worships at Ophrah, and it becomes a trap. Gideon has seventy sons, and a concubine in Shechem bears Abimelech. When he dies, Israel turns to Baal-berith and forgets both the LORD and Gideon's house (8:22–35).
readings: Read as a fall from grace

The hero of chapter 7 becomes, in chapter 8, a man who punishes his own people, takes private revenge, gathers gold and makes an object of worship. Many readers see the turning point in Gideon's career.
Read as an ambiguous hero

Others note that Succoth and Penuel betrayed Israel, that Gideon's refusal of kingship is genuine, and that the ephod may have been meant for inquiring of God. The narrator shows what came of it without fully judging his intent.

views.H: Traditional readers place Succoth and Penuel east of the Jordan near the Jabbok, towns linked with Jacob (Genesis 32–33). Gideon's refusal of kingship is taken as sincere, but the ephod as a real failure.
views.C: Critical scholars think the Transjordan pursuit (8:4–21) is a separate tradition from the Jezreel battle, perhaps a clan feud about Gideon's brothers. Gideon's refusal (8:22–23) is often read as an anti-monarchy saying added by the editor, since Gideon then acts like a king.
views.L: Literary readers point out that Gideon says no to the throne but behaves like a king: many wives, gold, royal purple, a cult center, and a son named Abimelech, "my father is king." His words and deeds point in opposite directions.
views.J: The rabbis debated the ephod. Some said Gideon meant it as a memorial or for inquiring of God, but Israel turned it into an idol. They praised his refusal of kingship as true humility.
views.X: Christian readers have used Gideon's ephod as a warning that even a victory given by God can become a trap when its trophies become objects of trust. Hebrews 11:32 still lists Gideon among the faithful, showing that faith and failure lived together in him.

deep.h: Did Gideon refuse to be king?
deep.b: Gideon's words in 8:23 are the Bible's first clear statement that the LORD alone should rule Israel. Samuel will say the same when Israel asks for a king (1 Samuel 8:7; 12:12). Yet many readers notice that Gideon goes on to act like a king, and that his son is named Abimelech, "my father is king." Some think Gideon's refusal was a polite formula, the way an ancient ruler might refuse a crown before taking power. Others think it was genuine but undone by his later choices. The next chapter shows what happens when his son accepts what Gideon refused.

deep.title: Claude's theory: gold for an ephod, gold for a calf
deep.b: My own reading: Gideon's ephod is told in the shape of Aaron's golden calf. Both leaders ask the people for their gold earrings, the people give freely, the leader makes an object, and the people worship it (Exodus 32:2–4). Both come right after a great rescue. If the parallel is deliberate, Gideon becomes an Aaron figure: a leader who meant well and made Israel sin. Some commentators mention the calf in passing; reading the scene as a full retelling of Exodus 32 is my own suggestion.

echoes: Genesis 32:30–31; Genesis 33:17; Exodus 28:6–14; Exodus 32:1–6; Deuteronomy 17:17; 1 Samuel 8:7; 1 Samuel 12:12; Psalm 83:11; Isaiah 9:4

settings.by: The men of Ephraim, and Gideon in reply
settings.to: Gideon; then the men of Ephraim
settings.when: after Ephraim captures Oreb and Zeeb
settings.why: Ephraim complains it was not called. Gideon answers with flattery: Ephraim's gleanings are better than his clan's whole harvest. Tribal anger is turned aside, unlike in 12:1–6, where Jephthah answers Ephraim with war.

settings.what: Gideon's threats to Succoth and Penuel
settings.by: Gideon, and the officials of Succoth and Penuel
settings.to: The towns of Succoth and Penuel east of the Jordan
settings.when: while chasing the kings of Midian
settings.why: When the towns refuse bread to his tired men, Gideon swears revenge. He later keeps his word. The rescuer of Israel now turns his anger on Israelites.

settings.what: Gideon and the kings of Midian
settings.to: The captured kings of Midian; then Gideon's firstborn Jether
settings.when: after the capture at Karkor
settings.why: Gideon asks about the men the kings killed at Tabor. They were his brothers, his mother's sons, and he swears by the LORD that he would have spared the kings had they spared them. He tells his young son to kill them, but the boy is afraid. The exchange shows a private blood feud behind the rescue of Israel. Readers see Gideon acting for his family as much as for the LORD.

settings.by: The men of Israel, and Gideon in reply
settings.to: Gideon
settings.when: after the defeat of Midian
settings.why: Israel asks Gideon to found a ruling family. He refuses: "The LORD will rule over you" (8:23). Yet he takes gold and makes an ephod that becomes a trap. He names a son Abimelech, "My father is king." For readers living under kings, the scene raises the book's question of who should rule.
views: Many read Gideon's words as a real confession that the LORD alone is king.
Others, such as Block and Webb, think his actions show he took power in fact while refusing the title.

title: Abimelech, the Bramble King
sum: Abimelech, Gideon's son by his Shechemite concubine, persuades Shechem to back him, hires killers with temple silver, and murders his seventy brothers on one stone. Only Jotham escapes. Shechem makes Abimelech king by the sacred oak (9:1–6). From Mount Gerizim Jotham tells a fable: the olive, fig and vine refuse to be king; only the thornbush accepts, threatening fire. He curses Shechem and Abimelech and flees (9:7–21).

After three years God sends a spirit of discord. Gaal son of Ebed stirs Shechem to revolt; Abimelech ambushes and destroys the town and sows it with salt, then burns a thousand people in the tower of El-berith (9:22–49). At Thebez a woman drops a millstone on his head, and he has his armor-bearer kill him. God repays Abimelech and Shechem, as Jotham said (9:50–57).
readings: Read as political warning
The chapter shows what kingship looks like when grabbed: murder, hired thugs, betrayal, and civil war. Jotham's fable is the Bible's sharpest satire of power.
Read as providence
No miracle appears and no judge rescues. God works only by sending discord and by repaying. The plot itself, with stone for stone and fire for fire, is God's justice.

views.H: Traditional readers see Abimelech as a real local tyrant, ruling Shechem and nearby towns. The destruction of Shechem fits excavated evidence of its destruction in the twelfth century BC, though the date of the great temple there is disputed.
views.C: Critical scholars see an old story from Shechem, probably close to events, set into the book without the usual frame. Shechem's history of strongmen and hired bands, from the Amarna letters on, gives it a believable setting. Jotham's fable may have been an independent piece used here.
views.L: Literary readers trace the chapter's symmetries: seventy killed on one stone, one stone kills Abimelech; fire threatened in the fable, fire at the tower, fire predicted between king and city. Every element of Jotham's curse comes true.
views.J: The rabbis drew the lesson that unworthy men seek office while worthy men refuse it, and read the fable as being about the leaders of each generation. Abimelech is the model of the son who betrays his father's good name.
views.X: Christian readers have used Jotham's fable as a warning against ambition in the church: those fit to lead are often busy bearing fruit, and those eager to rule have least to offer. Some preachers have contrasted the thornbush king with Christ, who wore a crown of thorns for others.

deep.b: Jotham's fable is often read as an argument against kings as such. The useful trees are too busy to rule; only the worthless bramble wants the job, and it threatens to burn those who do not submit. Martin Buber called it the strongest anti-monarchic poem in world literature. Yet Jotham's own speech after the fable is about Shechem's ingratitude to Gideon, not kingship in general. The book itself later longs for a king (17:6; 21:25). Many readers conclude that Judges distrusts a king grabbed by human ambition, while leaving room for one chosen by God.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the fable acted out in the plot
deep.b: My own reading: the second half of chapter 9 acts out the fable's details, not only its curse. The trees went out to anoint a king; Abimelech's men go out to the fields at harvest. The vine's wine cheers the drinkers at Shechem's festival (9:27). And when Abimelech cuts branches from the trees on Mount Zalmon to burn the tower (9:48–49), the trees literally become the fuel for the bramble king's fire. I suggest the narrator built the battle scenes to make the fable come true piece by piece. Scholars note that the curse is fulfilled; the claim that the trees' branches fulfill the fable is my own.

echoes: Genesis 12:6–7; Genesis 34:1–31; Genesis 35:4; Deuteronomy 27:12; Joshua 24:25–27; 2 Samuel 11:21; 1 Kings 12:1; 2 Kings 10:1–11; 2 Kings 11:1–3; 2 Kings 14:9

settings.to: His mother's brothers and the lords of Shechem
settings.when: after Gideon's death
settings.why: Abimelech asks whether it is better to be ruled by seventy sons of Jerubbaal or by one man, and reminds them that he is their own flesh and bone. The appeal to kinship and the promise of one ruler win Shechem to the first attempt at kingship in Israel.

settings.by: Jotham, Gideon's youngest son and the only survivor of the massacre
settings.to: The lords of Shechem, shouted from the top of Mount Gerizim
settings.when: on the day Shechem makes Abimelech king by the sacred oak
settings.why: The trees ask the olive, the fig and the vine to be king. Each refuses, because it has good work to do. Only the thornbush accepts, offering shade it cannot give and threatening fire. Jotham then asks whether Shechem acted in good faith. If it did not, he calls down a curse of fire. The fable mocks a king who is useless and dangerous. For readers under the monarchy it is a sharp warning against bad kings. The story that follows makes the curse come true (9:57).
views: Buber and others read the fable as one of the strongest anti-monarchy texts in the Bible.
Others think it attacks only Abimelech and Shechem's bad faith, not kingship itself.

settings.to: The people of Shechem at a harvest feast in their god's house
settings.when: after three years of Abimelech's rule
settings.why: Gaal asks who Abimelech is that Shechem should serve him, and boasts that he would remove him. The speech starts the revolt, and Zebul's taunt in 9:38 turns it against him.

title: Minor Judges and a Hard Repentance
sum: Tola of Issachar judges twenty-three years; Jair of Gilead judges twenty-two, with thirty sons on thirty donkeys holding thirty towns (10:1–5). Then Israel sinks lower than ever, serving the gods of seven peoples. The LORD sells them to the Philistines in the west and the Ammonites in the east, who crush Gilead for eighteen years and cross into Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim (10:6–9).

Israel cries out and confesses. God answers with a list of his past rescues and a refusal: "Go and cry to the gods you have picked." They confess again, put away their foreign gods, and serve the LORD, and the LORD can no longer bear Israel's misery. Ammon gathers in Gilead; Israel gathers at Mizpah, without a leader, and Gilead's chiefs offer headship to whoever will start the fight (10:10–18).
readings: Read as repentance
The chapter has the book's fullest scene of confession: words, then deeds. God's refusal tests whether Israel's cry is real, and the putting away of the gods shows that it is.
Read as exhaustion
Others read God's last line as weariness rather than pity: he has had enough of Israel's cycles. The leader who follows is chosen by the elders, not raised by God, and the results are mixed.

views.H: Traditional readers often see the Philistine and Ammonite oppressions as overlapping in time, one in the west (leading to Samson) and one in the east (leading to Jephthah), which would shorten the book's total years.
views.C: Critical scholars think 10:6–16 is a Deuteronomistic sermon introducing both Jephthah and Samson. The minor judges come from a separate list. Some think Jair's thirty towns are a version of the older tradition of Havvoth-jair (Numbers 32:41).
views.L: Literary readers see the low point of the cycle: seven sets of gods for seven rescues, and God refusing to rescue again. The chapter ends with Israel's leaders unable to lead, looking for any strongman who will fight.
views.J: The rabbis pointed to 10:16 as proof that God feels the suffering of Israel: "In every trouble of theirs, trouble came to him" (Isaiah 63:9). Rashi reads the end of 10:16 as God's compassion.
views.X: Christian readers have used this chapter to teach the difference between regret and true repentance, which turns from idols to serve the living God (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

deep.b: God's refusal in 10:13 is unique in the book. Some take it as a real limit reached, with God relenting only because of new evidence of repentance. Others see it as a test of sincerity, the way a parent says "no" to see whether a child means an apology. The prophets later report similar words: God tells Jeremiah not to pray for the people (Jeremiah 7:16; 11:14), and yet promises restoration. The chapter holds together God's anger and his compassion without resolving the tension.

echoes: Numbers 32:41; Deuteronomy 3:14; Deuteronomy 32:37–38; Genesis 35:2–4; Joshua 24:23; 1 Samuel 7:3–4; 1 Samuel 12:10; Jeremiah 2:28; Isaiah 63:9

settings.by: The Israelites, and the LORD in answer
settings.to: The LORD; then the Israelites
settings.when: after eighteen years under Ammon and the Philistines
settings.why: Israel confesses its sin. God answers with a list of his rescues and a refusal: "Go and cry to the gods you have picked" (10:14). Israel confesses again, puts away the foreign gods and serves the LORD. Then "the LORD had had enough of Israel's misery" (10:16). The exchange shows readers that repentance is more than a cry for help.
views: Many readers take 10:16 to mean that God could no longer bear to see Israel suffer, so his mercy wins over his anger.
Webb and others read the same words as impatience: God is worn out by Israel's cycle of sin and crying out, and acts without trusting its repentance.

settings.by: The leaders of Gilead, and Jephthah
settings.to: One another at Mizpah; then Jephthah in the land of Tob
settings.when: when Ammon gathers in Gilead and Israel has no leader
settings.why: With no leader, Gilead's chiefs offer headship to whoever will start the fight (10:18). The men who drove Jephthah out now need him. He bargains them up from field commander to head of all Gilead and seals the deal before the LORD at Mizpah. The scene shows a leader chosen by men, not raised up by God as earlier judges were.

title: Jephthah's Vow
sum: Jephthah, a Gileadite fighter born to a prostitute, is driven out by his half-brothers and gathers a band of "empty men" in Tob. When Ammon attacks, Gilead's elders come for him. He bargains them up from field commander to head of Gilead and seals the deal before the LORD at Mizpah (11:1–11). He sends the Ammonite king a long letter arguing from history that Israel took the land from Sihon, not from Ammon, and lets the LORD judge between them (11:12–28).

The Spirit of the LORD comes on Jephthah. He vows that whatever comes out of his house to meet him when he returns in victory will be the LORD's as a burnt offering. He wins. His only child, a daughter, comes out dancing with tambourines. She asks two months to mourn her virginity in the hills with her friends; then he does to her as he vowed. Israel's daughters retell her story every year (11:29–40).
readings: Read as tragedy

A man who bargained for everything bargains with God and loses the one thing he loved. The text never praises the vow and God never speaks. Most readers through history have taken it as a real sacrifice and a terrible mistake.
Read as dedication

Kimchi, Keil and Delitzsch and others have argued that Jephthah's daughter was dedicated to lifelong service and virginity, not killed: the vow can be read "or," "will be the LORD's" is dedication language, and the text stresses her virginity, not her death.

views.H: Traditional readers take Jephthah's letter as an accurate summary of Numbers 20–21 and his three hundred years as a real span. They differ on the vow: sacrifice, or dedication.
views.C: Critical scholars think the letter (11:12–28) was added to the story, since it seems to address Moab's god and land. Some see the daughter's story as explaining an old women's festival. Human sacrifice was practiced in the region, as 2 Kings 3:27 shows of Moab's king, and the story may reflect that world.
views.L: Literary readers compare the daughter's story with Isaac's: an only child, a father, a burnt offering, but no ram and no voice from heaven. They note that the daughter speaks with more faith and dignity than her father, and that her name is lost while her story is kept.
views.J: The rabbis condemned the vow. They said that if an unclean animal had come out he could not have offered it, and that he and the priest Phinehas were both too proud to meet and annul it, so both were punished (Genesis Rabbah 60:3). The Talmud lists Jephthah among those who asked improperly (Bavli Taanit 4a). Pseudo-Philo names the daughter Seila and gives her a lament.
views.X: Hebrews 11:32 includes Jephthah among the heroes of faith, for his faith in fighting, not for his vow. Augustine and most early Christian writers judged the sacrifice real and sinful; some medieval and later writers argued for dedication. Many modern Christians read the chapter as a warning against bargaining with God.

deep.b: The text says only that "he did to her the vow he had made" (11:39). Those who think she died, among them Josephus, Pseudo-Philo, the Targum, the rabbis, Augustine and most modern scholars, give three main arguments. First, the plain words of the vow: "I will offer it up as a burnt offering" (11:31), and "he did to her the vow he had made." Second, the narrator's echo of Isaac, the "one and only" child (11:34; Genesis 22:2), which leads the reader to expect a burnt offering. Third, the Bible knows no institution of lifelong celibacy for women at a sanctuary, so the dedication view must invent one. Those who think she lived, among them Joseph and David Kimchi, Keil and Delitzsch, Hengstenberg and many evangelical commentators, also give three. First, "will be the LORD's" is the language of dedication, as with Samuel (1 Samuel 1:11, 28), and the "and" of 11:31 can mean "or." Second, women served at the entrance of the tent of meeting (Exodus 38:8; 1 Samuel 2:22), and the law let a vowed person be redeemed (Leviticus 27:1–8), while it forbade human sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31). Third, she mourns her virginity, not her life, the narrator adds that she "had never slept with a man," and 11:40 can mean the daughters of Israel went yearly "to talk with" her. They add that Hebrews 11:32 lists Jephthah among the faithful. Modern readers such as Phyllis Trible have stressed that the narrator's silence is part of the horror, and that the women who remember her keep her story alive.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a man undone by his own skill
deep.b: My own reading: Jephthah's whole life is a series of verbal bargains. He bargains with the elders and wins (11:9); he argues with Ammon's king and is ignored (11:28); he bargains with God and wins the battle but loses his daughter; he argues with Ephraim and fights (12:1–4). I suggest the story shows a man whose one talent, getting the best terms with words, becomes his ruin when used on God, who had already given him the Spirit unasked. The narrator ends his career with a word test at the fords, where speech decides life and death (12:6). Scholars widely note Jephthah's skill at negotiation; reading the shibboleth as the last bargain in that series is my own.

echoes: Genesis 21:10; Genesis 22:1–14; Numbers 20:14–21; Numbers 21:21–35; Numbers 30:2; Leviticus 27:1–8; Deuteronomy 2:9; Deuteronomy 2:19; Deuteronomy 12:31; 2 Kings 3:27; 1 Samuel 12:11; Hebrews 11:32

settings.what: Jephthah's message to the king of Ammon
settings.to: The king of the Ammonites
settings.when: before the battle, after the king claims the land from the Arnon to the Jabbok
settings.why: Jephthah argues from history (Numbers 20–21). Israel took the land from Sihon king of the Amorites, not from Ammon or Moab. The LORD gave it to Israel, and Israel had held it for three hundred years. He ends by asking the LORD, "the Judge," to judge between them (11:27). The message tries to settle the dispute by right before war. For Israelite readers it defends their claim to the land east of the Jordan. The king does not listen.
views: The message names Chemosh, the god of Moab, as Ammon's god (11:24). Some think it mixes the two nations because the disputed land had been Moabite. Others think it was written later.
The number in 11:26 is used in debates over the dates of the exodus and the judges.

settings.to: The LORD
settings.when: after the Spirit of the LORD comes on him, before the battle
settings.why: Jephthah vows that whatever comes out of his house to meet him, when he returns in victory, will be the LORD's as a burnt offering. The Spirit has already come on him; the vow was not needed. For readers who knew the law against child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31; Deuteronomy 18:10), the vow is a terrible mistake.
views: Most ancient and many modern readers think he really offered his daughter.
Some medieval Jewish readers, such as Radak and Ralbag, and some Christians argue that she was given to lifelong service and never married (11:39).

settings.to: Each other
settings.when: as she comes out dancing to meet him
settings.why: Jephthah blames his daughter for his ruin. She tells him to keep his vow, and asks two months to mourn with her friends. Her calm courage stands against her father's rash words. A yearly mourning by the daughters of Israel kept her memory (11:39–40).

traditions.q: Must a rash vow be kept, and can the church release someone from a vow?
views: A vow binds only when it promises something good. Thomas Aquinas, following Jerome, said Jephthah was foolish in making his vow and wicked in keeping it (Summa II-II q88 a2). The Church can release a person from a vow for a good reason (Code of Canon Law 1196), and it honors lifelong religious vows as a high calling.
A vow that goes against God's command does not bind. The Augsburg Confession (article 27) rejected monastic vows made to earn grace, and Lutheran towns let monks and nuns leave their vows and marry.

No one may vow to do what God forbids, and such a vow must be broken, not kept (Westminster Confession 22.7). The same article calls lifelong vows of celibacy, poverty and obedience superstitious and sinful snares.

title: Shibboleth and Three Judges
sum: The men of Ephraim cross the Jordan to Jephthah, angry that he fought Ammon without them, and threaten to burn his house down. Jephthah answers that he did call them, and they did not come. War breaks out; Gilead defeats Ephraim and seizes the Jordan fords. Anyone who wants to cross is asked to say "Shibboleth"; those who say "Sibboleth" are killed, forty-two thousand in all (12:1–6). Jephthah judges six years and dies (12:7).

Three minor judges follow. Ibzan of Bethlehem has thirty sons and thirty daughters, married outside; Elon of Zebulun judges ten years; Abdon of Pirathon has forty sons and thirty grandsons on seventy donkeys (12:8–15).
readings: Read as civil war

For the second time Ephraim complains after a victory. Gideon soothed them; Jephthah fights them. The book's tribes now kill each other in larger numbers than their enemies, a step toward the war against Benjamin in chapters 20–21.
Read as quiet years
The minor judges that close the chapter show times of peace and wealth. Their large families riding donkeys suggest prosperity, though some readers see small dynasties forming, much like Gideon's.

views.H: Traditional readers take the Shibboleth test as a real event, showing a dialect difference between tribes on either side of the Jordan.
views.C: Critical scholars find the Shibboleth story an old tale preserving a real dialect feature. The minor judges come from the same list as Tola and Jair, and the editor placed them around Jephthah.
views.L: Literary readers notice how Ephraim's insult, "runaways," comes back on them at the fords. In a chapter about saying a word correctly, Jephthah's career ends as it went: by words that kill.
views.J: The Talmud identifies Ibzan with Boaz and says that all his sixty children died in his lifetime, because he did not invite Manoah, who was childless, to any of their weddings (Bavli Bava Batra 91a). A midrash says Jephthah's body fell apart limb by limb, each part buried in a different town.
views.X: Christian readers have used the Shibboleth as a picture of how speech reveals the heart (Matthew 12:34; 26:73), and of the danger of turning small differences into tests of belonging.

deep.b: The word shibbolet means "ear of grain" or "stream." Its first sound marked the speaker's home: Gileadites said "sh," Ephraimites apparently said "s." Since then "shibboleth" has entered English, and many other languages, for any password, test phrase or custom that marks who belongs. Similar tests are reported from many conflicts, where an enemy was identified by how he said a single word.

settings.by: The men of Ephraim, and Jephthah
settings.to: Jephthah; then the men of Ephraim
settings.when: after the victory over Ammon
settings.why: Ephraim threatens to burn Jephthah's house because he did not call them. He answers that he did, and they did not come. Then there is war, and the Shibboleth test. Unlike Gideon (8:1–3), Jephthah answers with the sword. The tribes now kill each other.
